problemStatement.formal: \text{Is computing } c^\nu_{\lambda,\mu} \text{ efficiently decidable? Formally: } c^\nu_{\lambda,\mu} \in \text{\#P-complete}
problemStatement.plain: Complexity of computing Littlewood-Richardson coefficients: positivity is in P via Knutson-Tao saturation; exact counting is #P-complete (Narayanan 2006). The 2-row case (Gr(2,4)) is provably polynomial time.
whyMatters: LR coefficients govern Schubert calculus, representation theory, and algebraic combinatorics
The P vs #P gap here is one of the sharpest complexity separations in combinatorics
Understanding which special cases are tractable guides algorithm design

proven: Positivity c^nu_{lam,mu} > 0 decidable in P: Knutson-Tao saturation + Klyachko inequalities (1998-1999)
For fixed number of rows k: polynomial time algorithm exists
open: Exact boundary between tractable special cases and #P-hard cases
Whether skew LR coefficients have the same complexity profile
knownResults.goal: Formalize the complexity dichotomy and the 2-row case in Lean

insights: Key convention: c^nu_{lam,mu} uses skew shape nu/mu (second factor) with content lam (first factor)
For 2-row SSYT, a tableau is uniquely determined by k1 = number of 1s in row 1
Column strictly increasing condition: for overlap columns, row1 must have 1 and row2 must have 2
Ballot condition reduces to: 2*k2 >= r2 where r2 is row 2 length of skew shape
The nontrivial zero sigma_2*sigma_11=0 comes from column condition: forces k2 <= 0 but range forces k2 >= 1
Gr(2,4) is multiplicity-free: all LR coefficients are 0 or 1 (proved by native_decide over 216 triples)
The P vs #P gap is witnessed by: positivity (P via LP) vs counting (sharp-P-complete via Narayanan 2006)
